segments: This is a video.
One click, and the mug is out of the frame. It has weight. It has a sound. This is a video you can touch.
We spend hours watching video, and all of it is read-only. SceneFork turns any paused video into a physical world you can touch, and reprogram by talking to it.
Here's a new clip, made with AI for this test. Open it, pause, fork.
Click the mug. SAM 3.1 outlines it from that one click.
Muse Image paints the table back in behind it.
Muse Spark works out what it's made of, and what it weighs.
Free the rest, and throw them. Each one sounds like what it is.
X-Ray shows the collision shapes and centers of mass the models just built.
Now change the laws of physics. Hold space, and talk.
The whole table lifts off.
Everything slams down. Moon and Mars are one click. Now point at the ball.
This means whatever you're pointing at.
Muse Voice gets you text in about half a second. Presets apply in under five milliseconds.
But what if the rule doesn't exist yet?
Muse Spark writes a small program, plus its own tests. A shadow copy of the world runs them before the rule can touch the real scene.
Here's the code, and the checks it had to pass.
Drag it back. Let go.
Not sure what to ask? Muse Spark suggests ideas from the scene. One tap, same tests. Rules stack, and removing one restores what was there.
It refuses, and tells you why. The AI proposes. The simulation decides.

Here's how it stays safe. New rules run first in a shadow world, in a worker with no network. A rule that does nothing is rejected. A failed test goes back to the model, up to twice. Stuck plugins die in three hundred milliseconds. On our demo scene, forty-eight of fifty generated rules passed. Built on React, Pixi and Rapier, with FastAPI and OpenCV.

Where this goes. A student films their own world, changes gravity, and sees the result, no lab, no code. A Reel becomes something viewers play with and remix by talking to it. A phone clip becomes a game prototype. The deepest idea: generated code proves itself in a shadow world before it touches the real one. That fits anywhere agents act on live systems. Physics runs on the viewer's device, so the main cost is model calls, about a cent and a half per object.
SceneFork. Any video becomes something you can touch. Built solo, in four days, on Meta's models. Open source, on GitHub.
